title: The poets of Anandpur
hookLine: tradition says he kept dozens of poets at his court

cards: Anandpur, in the hills. A town under threat for years, drilling soldiers, storing grain, watching the passes. And in the middle of it, tradition says, a room full of poets.
Dozens of them, gathered by Guru Gobind Singh, writing, translating, reciting. Under pressure, the extras usually get cut first. The Guru, by this memory, did the opposite.
You first visited this court on day eighty-three. Today is about that court, and about one poet whose words are still sung.

teach.b: Sikh tradition remembers the poets of Anandpur as a gathering of writers from different backgrounds: Sikhs and others, scholars of Sanskrit and of Persian.

teach.h: OPENING THE BOOKS, NOT GUARDING THEM.
teach.b: Tradition says the Guru set them to work bringing older works of story and wisdom into Braj, so that ordinary people could reach what had been locked in learned languages.

teach.h: LOST IN THE SARSA, TRADITION SAYS.
teach.b: Tradition also tells of a great collection of this work, sometimes called Vidya Sagar, the ocean of learning, and says much of it was lost in the flooded Sarsa river when Anandpur was left.
Nobody now can read what went under. One poet's work did survive, and Sikhs still sing it.
Bhai Nand Lal, called Goya, wrote in Persian, ghazals and couplets of love for the Guru.
Paraphrased, he writes of the Guru's face as the thing he longs to see, and of a single glance from the Guru being worth more than the world.
Sikh practice gives his poems a place in kirtan, alongside the Gurus' own hymns. Why would a Guru at war keep poets? Some readers answer: because what he was defending was not only land.
It was a way of life, and a way of life needs songs, stories and learning to carry it. Swords protect a people; poems tell them who they are.
The court of poets was the second half of the defense.

how: Sikhs sing the Persian ghazals of Bhai Nand Lal Goya in kirtan, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh's Anandpur as a center where poets and scholars translated and wrote.

practice: Pick any short poem, a hymn, a verse you learned as a kid, a song you know by heart, and say it out loud, slowly, once, listening to your own voice carry it.
Then sit quietly and let the last line keep sounding, and if you pray, let it lead you into Waheguru.
